newsitem.title: USA: Dow surges to second biggest point gain ever.
newsitem.headline: Dow surges to second biggest point gain ever.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average soared to its second biggest point gain ever Thursday amid a powerful rally in the bond market.
A suprise drop in the U.S. trade deficit sent the dollar higher, while tight supplies and frigid weather in the central United States sent oil and gas prices soaring.

In the stock market, the 30-stock Dow ended up 126.87 points, or 2 percent, at 6,473.64, its biggest rise since the blue-chip index soared 184.86 on Oct. 21, 1987 -- two days after crashing 508 points.
"This may be the start of the Santa Claus rally," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker.

On a percentage basis, however, Thursday's gains were not even in the top 10. In the broader market, advancing issues swamped declines 1,806 to 753 on heavy volume of 522 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 10.48 points to 1,295.86
Stocks were helped by a big rally in the bond market.

Thursday's economic reports, including a downbeat report from the Philadelphia Federal Reserve's business conditions survey for its region and a surprising rise in new jobless claims, sparked a big jump in long-term bonds and a drop in interest rates.

"The big surprise today was the decline in the Philly Fed survey," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany. "That was important because it was our first look at December numbers and it told us the economy was slower than in November," he said.
A slowing economy would reduce chances that the Federal Reserve would need to raise interest rates any time soon.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond jumped 1-1/2 points, or $15 per $1,000 face value, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, to 6.59 percent from 6.70 percent at Wednesday's close.
The dollar rose, helped by a surprise drop in the U.S. international trade deficit, which hinted the strong U.S. currency might not be damaging U.S. exports.

A jump in U.S. aircraft exports contributed largely to the 30.2 percent contraction in the October trade deficit in goods and services on Thursday. The overall trade gap narrowed to $7.99 billion from $11.44 billion in September.

Traders often purchase dollars when the deficit shrinks because it reduces the risk the government will try to weaken the currency to make exports cheaper abroad. In this case, the market got a much smaller gap than it expected.
The dollar ended at 1.5575 German marks, up from 1.5517 on Wednesday. Against the Japanese yen, the dollar made little headway after the data, because the bilateral trade gap with Japan widened.
The dollar rose to 114.03 yen from 113.69 yen.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange crude oil prices set a new post-Gulf War high for a second straight day, with January crude closing up 41 cents a barrel at $26.57.
January natural gas futures rose 33.4 cents to close at $4.409 per 1,000 cubic feet.

January heating oil, however, fell 0.40 cent a gallon to 73.78 cents as the freezing temperatures in the Midwest continued to skirt the Northeast, the world's largest heating oil market. January gasoline rose 0.05 cent a gallon to 71.22 cents on talk of scheduled maintenance at large refineries that will cut production.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 ended 33.1 points higher at 4,051.3. In Tokyo, the benchmark Nikkei 225 tumbled 522.36 points, the third largest one-day drop this year, to settle at 19,570.67.
